The town’s clockmaker retired on a Thursday and, for the first time in forty-three years, slept until he woke.

No bell. No chime. No small brass insistence from the bedside table.

He made coffee and stood at the kitchen window. Across the street, a boy was trying to teach a dog to jump over a broom. The dog regarded the broom as a problem best solved by walking around it.

“Quite right,” said the clockmaker.

For most of his life, he had repaired things that measured what could not be repaired. He had replaced springs, polished pivots, coaxed reluctant pendulums back into motion. Customers would hold a restored watch to their ear and smile.

That afternoon, he took the kitchen clock down.

There was a pale circle on the wallpaper behind it.

He had expected the room to look freer. Instead, it looked as though something had been stolen.

He stood holding the clock for a while, then put it back. It was twelve minutes slow. He reached for the minute hand, hesitated, and corrected it.

Retirement, apparently, would require practice.

Outside, the boy laid the broom on the pavement and stepped over it. The dog followed. The boy cheered so loudly that the clockmaker went to the window again.

By evening, they had raised the broom an inch.
